advances: The attained rank is the complete active-normal span for ordinary uniform volume, in a tapered body whose genuine marginal density is nonconstant.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The convex gauge $p_T$ and the Euclidean norm give a compact convex body with an inball. For $\|w\|\le1$, its $x$-section is $(1-\|w\|)T$, of volume $(1-\|w\|)^r|T|$. Hence
$$
|K|=q\omega_q |T|\int_0^1 b^{q-1}(1-b)^r\,db=\omega_q\frac{q!r!}{(q+r)!}|T|.
$$
The $w$-section over $x\in T$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $1-p_T(x)$, giving the density. The $x$-sections have centroid zero, and reflection in $w$ gives centroid zero in the other coordinates. Along each unit direction $e$ of the projection, set $t=s/p_T(e)$ in the radial integral. Then $\rho_0(e)^r$ is $p_T(e)^{-r}$ times the fixed positive factor $r\omega_q\int_0^1s^{r-1}(1-s)^q\,ds$, which proves the asserted dilation.

Each listed horizontal normal has a small apex cap in every positive-volume $x$-section, of relative volume $\Gamma_r$ by simplex homothety. These normals sum to zero. Their caps cover all points, so the maximum depth is at most $\Gamma_r|K|$. For any cap through zero with normal $(u,v)$ and $u\ne0$, put $F_u(s)=|T\cap\{u\cdot x\ge s\}|/|T|$. Pair the sections at $w$ and $-w$. For $\|w\|<1$ their thresholds in $T$ are opposite, $\pm v\cdot w/(1-\|w\|)$. Accepted fact 6a7d56e450b3126f gives a paired tail sum at least $2\Gamma_r$ because $T$ has centroid zero and $F_u$ is its normalized ordinary tail. The paired sections have the same volume, so the cap fraction is at least $\Gamma_r$. A purely vertical normal gives exactly $1/2>\Gamma_r$ by reflection. This establishes equality at zero.

If $u$ is not a positive multiple of a listed horizontal direction in $\mathbb R^r$, the equality characterization of the centroid inequality recorded in the proof of 03bc771bddd39a8a gives $F_u(0)>\Gamma_r$. In a simplex the equality cap must be on the apex side of a cut parallel to the opposite facet. Its normal is therefore one of the listed oriented directions. For noncanonical $u$, the paired excess stays strictly positive for all sufficiently small $w$ by continuity. For a canonical $u$, rescale so that its vertex values are $r,-1,\ldots,-1$. When $s$ is sufficiently small,
$$
F_u(s)+F_u(-s)=\frac{(r-s)^r+(r+s)^r}{(r+1)^r}.
$$
This is strictly greater than $2\Gamma_r$ when $s\ne0$ by strict convexity of the $r$th power on positive inputs. If $v\ne0$, the paired shift is nonzero for almost every small $w$. Integration gives strictness for these cases, so only the listed horizontal normals are active.

If a mark $(x_0,w_0)$ has $x_0\ne0$, some listed normal $u$ has $u\cdot x_0>0$ because they span and sum to zero. Its through-mark horizontal cap strictly loses mass from the origin cap, as seen on a positive-volume neighborhood of $w=0$ by the proper simplex cut at threshold zero. If $x_0=0$ and $w_0\ne0$, fix a canonical $u$ and use the through-mark normal $(u,t w_0)$ for $t>0$. In a section at $w$, its threshold is $t(\|w_0\|^2-w_0\cdot w)/(1-\|w\|)$. The simplex tail $F_u$ is globally Lipschitz by bounded parallel section areas, and $F_u'(0)<0$ by the apex-cap formula. With the section weight $(1-\|w\|)^r$, the derivative at $t=0$ may therefore be integrated by dominated convergence: the difference quotients are bounded by a constant times $(1-\|w\|)^{r-1}$ on the unit ball. The integral of the term involving $w_0\cdot w$ vanishes by reflection. The remaining derivative is $|T| F_u'(0)\|w_0\|^2\int_{\|w\|<1}(1-\|w\|)^{r-1}\,dw<0$. Thus a sufficiently small positive $t$ gives a cap of mass below $\Gamma_r|K|$. This proves uniqueness.

statement:
Fix integers $2\le r<d$, write $q=d-r$, and let $T$ be the centered simplex in $\mathbb R^r$ with vertices $-\mathbf1$ and $-\mathbf1+(r+1)e_i$ for $1\le i\le r$. Write $p_T$ for its Minkowski gauge, $\omega_q$ for unit $q$-ball volume, and let
$$
K=\{(x,w)\in\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^q:p_T(x)+\|w\|\le1\}.
$$
Its volume is $\omega_q q!r!|T|/(q+r)!$, and the pushforward of its volume onto $\mathbb R^r$ has density $\omega_q(1-p_T(x))^q\mathbf1_T(x)$. The origin is the unique ordinary deepest point, with normalized depth $\Gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r$. Its complete active menu, up to positive scaling, is $(e_i,0)$ for $1\le i\le r$ together with $(-\sum_{i=1}^r e_i,0)$. In particular, its complete active span has rank $r$. The projected radial body at zero is a positive dilate of $T$.
title: A tapered simplex body attains the sharp depth for its complete active rank
